## [2026-09-03] Individual Meritocratic Belief: hard-work item missing from 1999 — H1/H3 restricted to 2009/2019
**Context:** The Methodology Outline state the hard-work item (MAIN Individual Meritocratic Belief measure) is "available and coded consistently in all three waves" (1999/2009/2019).
The codebook shows this is false: the item (`v6` in the cumulation) is
explicitly marked "Variable not available in this module" for ISSP 1999 —
it only exists in 1987, 1992, 2009, and 2019. Cross-checked directly against
the 1999 questionnaire PDF (`ZA3430_bq.pdf`): the 1999 "getting ahead"
battery asked about wealthy family and knowing the right people only, not
hard work. Same problem, worse, for the ambition item (`v4`, the two-item
robustness measure's second component): available only in 1987/1992/2009 —
missing from BOTH 1999 and 2019, not just 2019 as previously assumed.
**Decision:** H1 and H3 (both use `ind_belief_c` as a moderator) are
restricted to the 2009 and 2019 waves only. 1999 is dropped from these two
models explicitly, not left in and relying on implicit listwise deletion — the 
sample restriction should be stated plainly in the methods/results write-up, not
buried. The two-item robustness check (hard work + ambition) is now a 
single-wave (2009-only) check, not a 1999/2009 comparison — `wave` was dropped 
from that model's formula since it would otherwise be a constant with no 
variation.
**Why this matters:** this shrinks the effective sample for the chapter's
two central, novel hypotheses (H1, H3) by a full wave and needs a
limitations-section footnote.

## [2026-10-26] Building from scratch: recodes verified against codebook labels
**Context:** Building the pipeline in a new repo (`CH1_recognition_injury`).
**Decision:** Every code (`sss`, `credential`, `ind_belief`, `income`, `gender`, 
`age`) was checked against the value labels and with old-vs-new cross-tabs 
before use. Negative codes (-9/-8/-7/-3/-1) → `NA`. `ind_belief` = 6 − `v6` (5 = 
strongest hard-work endorsement). Stratification direction checked
(Austria/Germany/Hungary = 8; Australia/Canada/NZ/USA = 0).

## [2026-10-27] ISEI missing for ~19.5% of respondents
**What I found:** Almost all are ISCO-88 missing codes (mainly -4: respondents 
with no job), not lookup gaps; code 110 (armed forces, 482 cases) is the only 
real unmatched code.
**Decision:** Left as `NA`. Non-working respondents drop out of any model with 
occupational status; this goes in the attrition table.

## [2026-10-27] Tertiary enrolment (WDI) missing for six sample country-waves
**What I found:** Australia, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Portugal and the USA 
have no `SE.TER.ENRR` value for 2006–2012 in the download, so none for the 2009 
wave. This is why the old main model had 25 countries (Portugal drops out 
entirely; Canada has only 1999).
**Decision:** Baseline keeps `tertiary` as `NA` (no interpolation). Five 
countries enter the main model with 2019 only. Planned sensitivity check: refit 
without `tertiary` as a control.

## [2026-10-27] Respondents aged 15–17 kept
**Decision:** Only `AGE = -9` set to `NA`. 455 respondents aged 15–17 and one 
aged 105 are retained. Restricting to 18+ is a possible sensitivity check.
  
## [2026-10-27] Analytic sample 
**Decision:** Sample built by sequential filters, recording n and countries after each step:
118,200 (35 countries) → waves 2009 + 2019: 87,019 (34) → has a stratification 
value: 60,945 (26) → complete on all model variables: 38,010 (25). 
Same as the old pipeline (25 countries,n = 38,010). `drop_na()` names the model 
variables explicitly. Canada leaves at the wave step (1999 only); the 8 
countries without OECD coverage leave at the stratification step; Portugal
leaves at the complete-case step (no 2019 wave, tertiary missing in 2009).

## [2026-10-27] Missingness is patterned by country and not by wave
**Result (26-country sample, before complete cases):** income missing 17.8% 
(largest loss), 7% (Norway) to 43% (Portugal); ISEI 12.7% (Spain 32%, Japan 31%); 
tertiary 12.7%. By wave: income 17.8% vs 17.9%; ISEI 14.6% (2009) vs 10.6% (2019). 
Income missingness is respondent non-response (-9/-8/-7), not an unasked item 
(no -1 codes in the high-missing countries). Individually lost respondents: 
income 10,857; ISEI 7,768; tertiary 7,732; sss 1,202; ind_belief 906; 
credential 672; age 408; gender 126 (overlap explains why they sum to more than 
the 22,935 lost).

## [2026-10-27] Retention by country is uneven
**Result:** complete-case retention ranges from 0% (Portugal) to 84% (Sweden). 
Australia keeps 658 respondents, Spain 486, Switzerland 3,077. Australia, 
Germany, Japan, USA and New Zealand contribute 2019 only (tertiary gap). The low 
end of stratification (Australia, NZ, USA) is hit hardest.

## [2026-10-27] Sensitivity sample without tertiary
**Result:** dropping `tertiary` from the complete-case rule gives n = 43,211 in 
26 countries (Portugal returns; five countries regain their 2009 wave). Planned 
as a robustness run.

## [2026-10-27] The analytic sample is selected
**Result:** sample at each step (2009/2019 data → 26 countries → complete cases): 
mean SSS 5.20 → 5.41 → 5.46; tertiary share 25.6% → 27.3% → 30.7%; 
mean age 48.4 → 50.2 → 50.9. The SSS rise comes from the country filter 
(the 8 dropped countries average SSS 4.70); the tertiary rise comes from the 
complete-case step.

## [2026-10-27] Univariate descriptives (n = 38,010)
**Result:** SSS mean 5.46, SD 1.72, range 1–10, roughly bell-shaped (histogram, binwidth 1).
Belief (1–5): mean 3.89, SD 0.90, median 4, upper quartile at the maximum (ceiling); 
+1 SD is about 0.9 of a scale point. ISEI mean 46.4 (SD 17.5, 16–90); 
age mean 50.9 (SD 16.3, 15–99). 30.7% tertiary; income terciles 32/33/35%; 
52.7% female; 45% 2009, 55% 2019.

**Plots:** SSS roughly bell-shaped; income terciles nearly even (top tercile slightly
over-represented); belief strongly left-skewed with mode at 4 (about 70% in categories 4–5,
only about 6% in 1–2); ISEI multimodal (clusters near 30, 50 and 70) because it takes
discrete values by occupation group. Limitation noted: few low-belief respondents.
